lede: You asked what else deserved a questionnaire and picked the table itself: how a roleplay session runs, from a turn's shape and length through Natalie's improvising, NPC wants and lies, Fronts and the Ledger, consequences, downtime, the Scene Menu and multiplayer on Discord. There are 43 questions in five sections, each with a recommendation you can take as it stands, and nothing ruled in the Style Law or the Combat Law is asked again: the settled list at the end says what was left alone and why. Answer the seven Keystones first, since most later questions lean on them.

question.title: What sways an NPC
question.question: Beyond its own want, what may decide how an NPC answers your PC's offer, threat or lie?
question.context: Table Rule 3: an NPC who would refuse, refuses. Table Rule 5 decides from 'Stage gap, the read, what has been spent, and the environment' (R14-3), but every stat row is a fight's or a working's, and R71-22 prices a lie only mid-fight. Nothing weighs your PC's rank, name or lie in talk. Old-school tabletop rolled an NPC's reaction; WOTR rolls nothing (R13-8).

options.label: Rank bends it
options.consequence: A Stage gap felt as Pressure (R70-69) and a commoner's awe of a ranked practitioner (R53-18) can make an NPC yield what its want alone would refuse; a ranked NPC weighs them less.

options.label: His name goes before him
options.consequence: Ledger lines for reputation and who saw what reach the NPC: it answers what your PC did in public, for good or ill, and the notes name the line that weighed.

options.label: His lies caught on evidence
options.consequence: An NPC catches your PC's lie only on what it can check: a tell in his body, a fact it holds, or a read its Gnosis earns (R14-3's read row). Otherwise the lie holds.

question.rec_reason: All three carry Table Rule 5's own inputs into talk (the gap, his record, the read), so a social outcome reconstructs as a fight's does (R13-8), and his lie stands or falls on evidence you could manage, never on what Natalie knows.

question.title: Who writes the close
question.question: When a session closes, does Natalie apply what it writes to the table, or does each item wait for your yes?
question.context: The wotr-ledger and judger skills make every Ledger line, Front tick and roster entry 'a proposal Isaac approves item by item'. Three judger closes made 115 proposals and 22 landed; sessions.yaml logs one session, and the Kharven State of Play was last rewritten 2026-09-10. Your direction is that nothing waits on you, and R20C-34 says estimates no longer wait for ratification.

options.label: Each item waits
options.consequence: As the skills say now: at your wrap Natalie drafts the close, and every Ledger line, Front tick, roster entry and State of Play change waits for your yes.

options.label: Applied, then listed
options.consequence: At your wrap and whenever a scene is archived, Natalie applies the close herself and lists each write once as an agent ruling (a call you may overturn); nothing waits.

options.label: Applied, yours wait
options.consequence: As B, except a write that sets a fact about your own characters (their body, kin, Stage or a choice) waits for one word from you, as K2's option B does in play.

question.rec_reason: It ends the close that never lands and matches the call K2 recommends for play, keeping back only what is yours (R52-08); a scene archived is a scene closed, so the State of Play stops going stale.

question.title: Scenes set in the past
question.question: When a scene is set before its thread's live moment, what may it write to the Fronts and the Ledger?
question.context: The Kharven Fronts are keyed to the year after, yet most Kharven scenes archived since are backfill (written later, set earlier) of the Ashgate day; their costs went onto the Ledger beside live ones, and one line waits on a man another scene killed. R53-09 dates each thread on its State of Play. ME2 sorts the old rows; this sets the rule going forward.

options.label: Only what still binds
options.consequence: A past scene adds canon and precedent, and writes a Ledger line or Front history only for what still binds at the thread's live date, which the close checks.

options.label: Dated, then retired
options.consequence: A past scene writes Ledger lines and Front history dated to its own day; any line already paid or moot by the live date retires at once with a note.

options.label: Canon only
options.consequence: A past scene writes nothing to the table; what it set up reaches play only when a live scene picks it up.

question.rec_reason: It keeps due() honest about where the thread stands while the costs a past scene really carries forward (a scar, a debt still open) reach the table at once, and nothing is entered only to be retired.

rec_changes.rec_reason: The read is the game (Table Rule 6) and you like counters that can be found; a sign for every tick gives you something to find, and owning the files leaves you free to look whenever you choose.

Story time is already tracked (R53-09) and a trigger in the fiction is how a debt really arrives; with a thread on every row and the fired lines marked, due() stops handing you thirty lines from every thread at once.

Money before magic (R53-17) and a named sum for every payment (R70-48) want living costs on the page, your LitRPG models love visible progress, and a clock shows long work without inventing a number; cooling heat and keeping a bond stay on the list only if WD5 adds them.

The read stays the game wherever your character could make it; a death he could never have read gets one plain line in the foot, as fair play already says (never punish you for what nobody could find), and that is what R48-31's 'clear warning' is for.

The world moved before him and moves after him; keeping the clocks and handing the debts on makes the death cost something in the world, and leaves you free to choose who walks in next, an heir included.
Guest players get a world that answers under the same law as the Desktop table, while you keep every word that reaches the server and the bot stays as you decided.

Guests did not sign your Floor, so their own limits and their character's mortality are theirs to set, and Discord requires age-restricted channels anyway; out-of-character brackets already serve as a pause.

A flag nobody rules sits forever, against your 'nothing waits' direction; one struck-or-accepted mark settles each break, and owner marks keep other players' characters from being written by mistake (R52-10).
The lines record real costs from real scenes and your direction is that nothing sits pending; one pass makes due() usable at once without throwing away what play already paid for.

intros.WD: How the world moves when your PC is not looking: Fronts (threats with a want and a clock of four to six ticks), the Ledger (the running bill of wounds, debts, witnesses and reputation), what sways an NPC and what NPCs do between scenes, time off, the road, what the world pays or takes, and the session close that writes it all down. The prose samples, in WD4, follow an invented Kharven courier-rider, Aske, standing in for a player's character.
intros.MP: The Discord table: your server, where players post as their own characters through Tupperbox (a bot that posts under a character's name) and you sit as Judger, the role that rules and enters canon. R71-6 already settles how a guest's fighter appears on the page; these questions cover the rest.

settled_extra.point: Every character you play is yours under R49-01, R52-08 and R52-10, the Academy roster of ten on Discord included; 'your PC' in these questions means whichever of them is on the page.
settled_extra.why_not_asked: R52-10 already speaks of your POV characters in the plural, and the archive treats all ten as yours; no option here narrows it.

settled_extra.point: When your own finished text contradicts a Front or a Ledger line, the text stands and the table is corrected to it, as the Wren Front was recast as a grief Front after The War in the North IV.
settled_extra.why_not_asked: The canon hierarchy puts your direction first, and the Wren recast of 2026-09-26 is the precedent; WD15 asks only what a scene set in the past writes to the table.

notes: 1. Read both groups (40 questions, 49 settled rows) and the three research files, and checked every cited rule id against rules/*.yaml (all exist) and the cross-references to the mystery, intimacy and techniques questionnaires' current group files. 2. No drops: no two questions ask the same thing. Close pairs kept and cross-referenced: K5 with the intimacy SC13 (standing orders in bed); K6 with the mystery HO3 and intimacy SC12; K7 with the mystery K7 (cuts inside a case); WD2 with the mystery IN6 (intrigue Fronts' visibility; IN6 recommends a shown clock with sealed contents, WD2 hidden clocks with open files, so the main session should reconcile the two recommendations when both are answered); WD6 with the mystery K5, MY9, MY10; WD7 with the techniques CH12; WD8 with the techniques CH15. 3. Three additions, each a gap research-law or research-house flagged and no group asked: WD13 what sways an NPC (social adjudication: R14-3's rows are all fight rows and nothing weighs Pressure, reputation or the PC's own lie in talk); WD14 who writes the session close (the skills' item-by-item approval against the nothing-waits direction; 115 judger proposals, 22 applied; it also fixes the close's trigger at a wrap or an archived scene, so no separate 'what is a session' question was needed); WD15 scenes set in the past (backfill writing Ashgate-day costs beside the year after). 4. Recommendations aligned: WD14 C matches K2 B; WD11 B now points at TU5's OOC foot instead of the 'chat summary'; WD8's rec notes that heat and bonds depend on WD5. Recommended options unchanged; nine rec_reasons rewritten only to address you directly. 5. Voice: group-2 named Isaac in the third person in its questions, contexts, consequences and reasons; text_fixes and rec_changes turn those to 'you', as group-1 and the earlier questionnaires do ('he' and 'his' for the PC are kept). WD and MP intros rewritten the same way, WD's to name the three additions. 6. Stale text: group-2's settled row had the mystery ids wrong (catching a lie is its K5, the uncaught lie MY10, honest errors MY9); group-1's italic-thought row said 'per turn' where Table Rule 10 and R48-40's allowance read per scene. 7. Settled list deduped: eight group-2 rows repeated group-1 rows (NPC voices, the hook reward and penalty, numbers for a shown cause, the warm bond, standing orders, a player's fighter, the sign and exit, NPC thoughts); they are removed by multi-line text_fixes (each old string is the row's exact text with its leading comma) and their cross-references folded into group-1's rows. Two settled_extra rows: every character Isaac plays is his PC (the Discord roster of ten), and his own finished text outranks a Front or a Ledger line. 8. Every text_fix was applied in order to scratch copies: each old string occurs exactly once at its turn, both files parse, and the merged set checks clean (43 questions, no dashes, 2 to 4 options, labels 5 words or fewer, consequences under 40 words, contexts under 70 words, every depends_on resolves).
